screens.title: What is Game State?
screens.narratorSegment: Game state is the collective set of variables that describe everything the game needs to continue operating from this exact moment. Concretely, that includes player attributes like position, health, current weapon and inventory, but it also includes enemy statuses, active quests, level index, timers, and environmental modifiers such as day/night or weather. If you paused the game and wrote down every internal value required to resume later, you would have captured the game state. This matters because a well-designed state model makes saving, networking and deterministic replay tractable. A common misconception is to equate game state only with visible elements on screen; invisible timers, AI memory and input buffers are also part of state. Another misconception is to scatter state across global variables and ad‑hoc flags. That leads to fragile code: it's hard to reason about order of updates and to avoid contradictory values. An example: storing player position as three floats is fine, but storing movement as multiple loose booleans like isMoving and isWalking invites conflicts. The better approach is to list every needed field, group related fields into structures, and treat the game snapshot as the single source of truth when pausing, saving, or replicating. Reflect: what minimal fields would you need to save to fully restore a level in your current project?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Game state is the complete snapshot of all variables the game needs to resume or reason about the current moment.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is Game State?

The complete set of internal values that determine the game's current snapshot. Includes visible and invisible values.

Concrete example
Player position, health, inventory; enemy positions and health; active quests; level index; timers and AI states.
Common misconception
Only what’s visible matters — false. Hidden timers and AI memory are part of state too.
Why it matters
A clear state model simplifies saving, network sync and debugging because the snapshot becomes a single source of truth.
Key Takeaway

Think of game state as the single snapshot you would need to save and later restore the exact running game.

Grouped state checklist
  • Player: position, velocity, health, currentWeapon, inventory.
  • Enemies: position, currentState, health, aggro timers.
  • World: level index, time of day, active environmental effects.
  • Systems: input buffers, event queues, spawn timers, save flags.
Analogy
Photograph of the world
A saved snapshot recreates the scene exactly later.
Try this
List minimal save fields
Try exporting only necessary data for a simple level and test restore.

screens.title: Modeling State with C++ Types
screens.narratorSegment: Representing game state in C++ begins with choosing the right building blocks. Primitive types like int and float are perfect for single, simple values such as a score or health. But once values are related — positionX, positionY, velocity — grouping them into a struct or class makes your code clearer and safer. For example, a Player struct can hold position, health, and inventory references so systems accept a single object instead of many separate parameters. A class adds encapsulation and methods, letting you keep invariants like clamping health inside the class rather than repeating logic across systems. Enums complement these types by providing named constants for discrete categories, which we’ll use shortly for states. A common beginner error is to keep many globals or pass dozens of primitives between functions; grouping fields reduces parameter lists and avoids inconsistent updates. As an example, a Player class with methods like TakeDamage or ChangeWeapon centralizes side effects and helps maintain a valid state. When designing types, prefer composition: make a Position struct inside Player rather than having global X and Y values. This approach makes saving, copying and testing simpler because you can serialize or clone a single object.

keyIdea.text: Group related fields into structs/classes and put behavior that maintains invariants inside those types for clearer, safer code.

content.html:
Representation

Modeling with primitives, structs, and classes

Choose primitives for single values, structs to group data, and classes when you need methods and encapsulation.

When to use a struct
Group related data like position and velocity into a Position or Physics struct for clarity and reuse.
When to use a class
Encapsulate behavior such as TakeDamage, Heal, or ChangeWeapon so the object enforces valid state changes.
Key Takeaway

Prefer grouping related fields and keeping state logic inside types to reduce bugs and duplication.

Example: Player skeleton
// C++ style pseudocode
struct Position {
  float x;
  float y;
};

class Player {
public:
  Position pos;
  int health;
  void TakeDamage(int amount) { health -= amount; if (health <= 0) OnDeath(); }
private:
  void OnDeath();
};
Pro tip
Keep invariants inside methods
Let the class clamp health and manage side effects like death or animation flags.
Common mistake
Too many globals
Scattering related fields across the codebase makes reasoning and saving harder.

screens.title: Using enums to name discrete states
screens.narratorSegment: Enums are a simple but powerful C++ feature for naming a fixed set of options. When modeling states, an enum gives you readable labels such as Idle, Walking, Jumping, Attacking, and Dead. Compared to magic numbers or strings, enums are type-safe, easier to refactor, and far less error‑prone. For example, testing if currentState == PlayerState::Jumping is clearer and safer than checking an integer code or comparing strings at runtime. A common misconception is that enums are only for small values; in games they act as the canonical list of allowed states, making it explicit what an entity can do. Enums also make debugging easier because the names show up clearly when converted to strings for logging. One limitation to note: if you need many combinations of simultaneous properties, enums alone are not the right tool—use them to represent mutually exclusive states. For orthogonal properties like 'isInvincible' or 'hasDoubleJump', keep separate booleans or flags, but be careful to avoid contradictory combinations. The key is to use enums for the primary mode of an entity and separate fields for independent modifiers. Using enums to name discrete states means use enums to represent mutually exclusive states clearly and safely; avoid using them for independent modifiers.. In practical terms, why enums beat magic numbers and strings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enum advantage
keyIdea.text: Use enums to represent mutually exclusive states clearly and safely; avoid using them for independent modifiers.

content.html:
Definition

Enums for discrete states

Enums name the finite set of modes an entity can occupy and make checks readable and type-safe.

enum class PlayerState {
  Idle,
  Walking,
  Running,
  Jumping,
  Attacking,
  Dead
};
Enums should represent mutually exclusive modes. For independent modifiers, use separate flags to avoid conflating concepts.
Why enums matter
  • Readability: names show intent clearly in code and logs.
  • Safety: the compiler can catch invalid assignments when using scoped enums.
  • Maintainability: adding a new state centralizes changes rather than sprinkling magic numbers.
Misuse to avoid
Using enums for combinations of unrelated properties. If states can co-exist, use flags or separate fields instead.

screens.title: Finite State Machine (FSM) Basics
screens.narratorSegment: A finite state machine is a clear, mathematical pattern for modeling behavior where an entity can be in exactly one of a finite set of states at any time. The FSM pattern has three parts: a list of states (usually an enum), rules to change from one state to another (transition guards), and state-specific behavior executed each update. In games, this maps directly to behaviors like Idle, Walking, Jumping and Attacking. The ChangeState method enforces transition rules — for example, preventing switching out of Dead — and can run entry and exit actions like starting or stopping animations. The Update method inspects currentState and executes only the logic for that state. This organization prevents contradictory behavior such as being both Idle and Attacking when not permitted. A common misconception is that FSMs remove all complexity; they don't. FSMs reduce complexity by centralizing state logic, but you still need to design transitions and consider orthogonal modifiers such as temporary invincibility. As a simple exercise, imagine an enemy that can patrol, chase, and attack: the transitions occur when player proximity crosses thresholds. FSMs make those rules explicit and easier to maintain.

keyIdea.title: FSM pattern
keyIdea.text: Use an enum for states, guard transitions in ChangeState, and run state behavior in Update to prevent invalid combinations.

content.html:
Pattern

Finite State Machine

States, guarded transitions, and update-time behavior. This prevents contradictory flags and centralizes logic.

Step 1
Define states as an enum
Step 2
Implement ChangeState with guards
Step 3
Run state-specific logic in Update
Concrete scenario
Player transitions from Idle to Walking when movement input exists, to Jumping when jump input occurs, and to Dead when health reaches zero. ChangeState enforces that Dead cannot transition back to non-dead states.
Misconception
FSMs automatically fix bugs — they help prevent certain bugs but require thoughtful transition design.

keyIdea.title: Code pattern
keyIdea.text: A Player FSM organizes state, transition guards, and state-specific updates in one place for easier debugging and extension.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

enum class PlayerState {
  Idle,
  Walking,
  Running,
  Jumping,
  Attacking,
  Dead
};

std::string PlayerStateToString(PlayerState state) {
  switch (state) {
    case PlayerState::Idle: return "Idle";
    case PlayerState::Walking: return "Walking";
    case PlayerState::Running: return "Running";
    case PlayerState::Jumping: return "Jumping";
    case PlayerState::Attacking: return "Attacking";
    case PlayerState::Dead: return "Dead";
    default: return "Unknown";
  }
}

class Player {
public:
  Player() : currentState(PlayerState::Idle), health(100) {}

  void ChangeState(PlayerState newState) {
    if (currentState == newState) return;
    if (currentState == PlayerState::Dead && newState != PlayerState::Dead) {
      std::cout << "Cannot change state from Dead unless it's still Dead.
";
      return;
    }
    std::cout << "Player transitioning from " << PlayerStateToString(currentState)
              << " to " << PlayerStateToString(newState) << ".
";
    currentState = newState;
  }

  void Update(double deltaTime) {
    switch (currentState) {
      case PlayerState::Idle:
        // idle logic
        break;
      case PlayerState::Walking:
        // walking logic
        break;
      case PlayerState::Jumping:
        // jumping logic
        break;
      case PlayerState::Attacking:
        // attacking logic
        break;
      case PlayerState::Dead:
        // death logic
        break;
      default:
        break;
    }
  }

  void TakeDamage(int amount) {
    health -= amount;
    if (health <= 0) {
      health = 0;
      if (currentState != PlayerState::Dead) ChangeState(PlayerState::Dead);
    }
    std::cout << "Player took " << amount << " damage. Health: " << health << "
";
  }

private:
  PlayerState currentState;
  int health;
};
Reading guide
  • Note the enum names as the canonical set of states.
  • ChangeState contains a guard preventing non-sensical transitions from Dead.
  • Update holds the place for state logic — keep behavior here to avoid scattered conditionals.
Dev tip
Add logging inside ChangeState while developing to trace unexpected transitions quickly.

screens.title: ChangeState: Guards and Entry/Exit Logic
screens.narratorSegment: ChangeState is the gatekeeper for your FSM. It decides when transitions are allowed, runs optional exit logic for the old state and entry logic for the new state, and updates the current state variable. A minimal ChangeState checks for no-op transitions first and returns if the state is already the same. Next, include guards to prevent invalid transitions — for example, avoid moving out of Dead unless your design supports resurrection explicitly. Implementing entry and exit hooks lets you stop the previous animation, reset movement variables, and start the new animation and sound effects consistently. A common mistake is to mix entrance logic into Update or other systems, which scatters responsibilities and leads to subtle timing bugs. For example, if you start an attack animation in Update and also in ChangeState, you may trigger it twice. Structure ChangeState so it does only state transition tasks and leave continuous per-frame behavior to Update. As a practical check, add debug prints to ChangeState during development and verify that each transition happens only once when expected. How would you implement an onEnter and onExit system for each state in your codebase?

keyIdea.title: Transition control
keyIdea.text: Use ChangeState to enforce valid transitions and run entry/exit actions; keep per-frame behavior inside Update.

content.html:
Process Flow

ChangeState responsibilities

  1. Check if newState == currentState and return if so.
  2. Run exit logic for currentState (stop animation, reset temporary variables).
  3. Guard invalid transitions (e.g., Dead → non-Dead).
  4. Assign currentState = newState and run entry logic (start animation, reset timers).
Example guard
If currentState == Dead and newState != Dead then ignore or handle resurrection explicitly.
Entry / Exit hooks (pattern)
Implement small onEnter and onExit helper methods for each state and call them from ChangeState to keep code modular. This avoids repeating animation or sound logic across other systems.
Common mistake
Doing per-frame logic in ChangeState
ChangeState runs on transitions; per-frame updates belong in Update to avoid missed or duplicated behavior.

screens.narratorSegment: The Update method executes the logic appropriate to the entity’s current state on every frame. Implement Update with a switch on currentState so each state’s behavior is grouped together. For instance, in Walking you apply movement velocity and play a walking animation, while in Jumping you apply a vertical impulse and track airborne time. This keeps state code localized and avoids conditionals scattered across the codebase. Include short comments or placeholder calls for physics, animation, and collision checks so you remember to add those systems later. One misconception is to put logic that should run in multiple states into separate places; instead, factor shared behavior into helper methods you can call from multiple cases. Also be mindful of performance: keep Update cases focused and offload heavy work, like pathfinding, to less frequent systems or background tasks. As an example, the Jumping case can increment a jumpTimer and automatically call ChangeState to Idle when the timer exceeds a configured duration. keyIdea.text: Use Update to perform per-frame, state-specific behavior and timers, keeping shared functionality in helpers.

content.html:
Implementation

Update switch example

void Player::Update(double deltaTime) {
  switch (currentState) {
    case PlayerState::Idle:
      // regenerate stamina or wait for input
      break;
    case PlayerState::Walking:
      // apply walking velocity, play walking animation
      break;
    case PlayerState::Jumping:
      // increment jumpTimer, apply gravity, check landing
      jumpTimer += deltaTime;
      if (jumpTimer >= JUMP_DURATION) {
        ChangeState(PlayerState::Idle);
      }
      break;
    case PlayerState::Attacking:
      // perform attack checks, spawn hitboxes
      break;
    case PlayerState::Dead:
      // disable input and play death sequence
      break;
  }
}
Notes and checks
  • Keep Update fast; avoid heavy calculations each frame.
  • Store timers like jumpTimer as members and reset them on state entry.
  • Use helper functions for shared logic to avoid duplication.
Practical check
Simulate Update with a fixed delta to verify timed transitions behave as expected in console logs.

screens.title: Add Timed Jump Logic (Activity)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through adding realistic jump timing to the Player FSM. The goal is to prevent transitioning from Jumping to Idle immediately; instead, the Player should remain in Jumping until a jump duration elapses. Start by adding a float member jumpTimer initialized to zero and a constant JUMP_DURATION, for example 0.8 seconds. Modify ChangeState so entering Jumping resets jumpTimer to zero. Then update the Jumping case in Update to increment jumpTimer by deltaTime each frame and check whether it exceeds JUMP_DURATION; if so, call ChangeState to go to Idle or Walking. This pattern simulates time in the air and enables other checks such as disabling double jumps until the timer allows it. A common pitfall is forgetting to reset jumpTimer when re-entering Jumping, which can cause the player to land immediately. After implementing, simulate frames in main with a fixed delta and print state transitions to verify behavior. This exercise demonstrates how FSMs and timers interact to produce believable movement, and practicing it will make adding other timed actions like attack windup or cooldowns straightforward. screens.title: FSMs vs. Boolean Flags
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often model behavior with multiple booleans: isWalking, isJumping, isAttacking. At first this seems simple, but these flags can combine into contradictory states — for example, both isWalking and isJumping true unless special code prevents it. FSMs, by contrast, enforce a single canonical mode so such contradictions cannot arise without explicit design. FSMs centralize state logic in one place, improving readability and making it easier to add or change behaviors. That said, booleans still have a place: for independent modifiers like isInvincible or hasDoubleJump, flags are appropriate. The comparison is: FSMs for mutually exclusive primary modes, flags for orthogonal modifiers. A second advantage of FSMs is maintainability: adding a new mode means adding a single enum value, a case in Update, and any necessary transition rules in ChangeState. With booleans you must find every location that sets or reads flags and update them, increasing the chance of bugs. As a concrete test, try converting a system that used booleans into an FSM and notice how many fewer cross-checks you need. Which parts of your current project better fit an FSM and which should remain as flags?

FSMs vs Boolean Flags

content.html:
Assessment Idea

Enemy FSM design

Write an enum, currentState, ChangeState, and Update implementing Patrolling → ChasingPlayer → Attacking transitions based on proximity checks.

enum class EnemyState { Patrolling, ChasingPlayer, Attacking };

class Enemy {
  EnemyState currentState = EnemyState::Patrolling;
  void Update(double dt, const Player& p) {
    switch (currentState) {
      case EnemyState::Patrolling:
        // move along path
        if (IsPlayerNearby(p)) ChangeState(EnemyState::ChasingPlayer);
        break;
      case EnemyState::ChasingPlayer:
        // move toward player
        if (IsWithinAttackRange(p)) ChangeState(EnemyState::Attacking);
        else if (!IsPlayerNearby(p)) ChangeState(EnemyState::Patrolling);
        break;
      case EnemyState::Attacking:
        // attack logic
        if (!IsWithinAttackRange(p)) ChangeState(EnemyState::ChasingPlayer);
        break;
    }
  }

  void ChangeState(EnemyState newState) { /* log and set currentState with guards */ }
};
Evaluation
Correct transition example
Patrolling to ChasingPlayer triggered by a proximity check is required to demonstrate understanding.
Why this works
Explicit transitions prevent oscillation and conflicting behavior when player distance fluctuates briefly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll explore what “game state” really means for a C++ game and why a clean structure makes your code easier to build and debug. Game state is every variable that describes the world right now: player health and position, enemy status, score, current level, active quests, and even environmental factors like time of day. Treating these values as one coherent snapshot is essential. You will learn practical ways to represent state in C++: primitives for simple values, structs and classes for grouped data, and enums for clear, bug‑resistant state labels. We will then build a basic finite state machine for a Player character: an explicit set of states, rules to change between them, and state‑specific behavior in the game loop. I’ll show concrete code patterns you can copy into your projects and common beginner mistakes to avoid, such as using scattered booleans that lead to contradictory states. By the end, you’ll understand why an FSM improves readability, prevents invalid behavior, and makes adding new actions, like a dash or a timed jump, straightforward. Think about a moment in your game where two systems conflict; we’ll show how state design removes those conflicts.

These objectives guide what to practice and why it matters. First, you will be able to define what we mean by game state in a C++ context. That means recognizing every variable that contributes to the current game snapshot and understanding why saving or copying that snapshot matters for features like pause, save games, or network synchronization. Second, you will design simple C++ types—primitives, structs, classes and enums—to represent related groups of state cleanly. This skill helps reduce scattered variables and allows you to reason about entities as single units. Third, you will implement a basic finite state machine for a game entity, learning the pattern of defining states, writing a ChangeState method, and using an Update loop to run state logic. Finally, you'll understand benefits of FSMs: they prevent invalid combinations of behaviors and make adding new actions safer. For each objective you’ll see a small mnemonic and a competency milestone to confirm you can apply the idea to your own game code.

These milestones turn concepts into measurable tasks. You will be able to identify every field that must be saved to recreate a game snapshot, for example exporting player position, health, inventory, and level progress. You will also design a small Player class with grouped properties rather than scattered globals, which simplifies passing the player object to systems like rendering or physics. Another milestone is writing an enum to name discrete states and updating an entity’s currentState variable through a ChangeState method that checks for invalid transitions. Finally, you will write Update logic that runs only the behavior appropriate for the current state and add a timed jump mechanic that prevents immediate landing. Each task helps you move from reading to coding, making debugging and future extension far easier. Learning Objectives — Practical Milestones means complete small coding tasks: snapshot fields, player class, enum states, changestate guards, update loops and timed jump logic.. In practical terms, concrete tasks to verify understanding. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Game state is the collective set of variables that describe everything the game needs to continue operating from this exact moment. Concretely, that includes player attributes like position, health, current weapon and inventory, but it also includes enemy statuses, active quests, level index, timers, and environmental modifiers such as day/night or weather. If you paused the game and wrote down every internal value required to resume later, you would have captured the game state. This matters because a well-designed state model makes saving, networking and deterministic replay tractable. A common misconception is to equate game state only with visible elements on screen; invisible timers, AI memory and input buffers are also part of state. Another misconception is to scatter state across global variables and ad‑hoc flags. That leads to fragile code: it's hard to reason about order of updates and to avoid contradictory values. An example: storing player position as three floats is fine, but storing movement as multiple loose booleans like isMoving and isWalking invites conflicts. The better approach is to list every needed field, group related fields into structures, and treat the game snapshot as the single source of truth when pausing, saving, or replicating. Reflect: what minimal fields would you need to save to fully restore a level in your current project?

Representing game state in C++ begins with choosing the right building blocks. Primitive types like int and float are perfect for single, simple values such as a score or health. But once values are related — positionX, positionY, velocity — grouping them into a struct or class makes your code clearer and safer. For example, a Player struct can hold position, health, and inventory references so systems accept a single object instead of many separate parameters. A class adds encapsulation and methods, letting you keep invariants like clamping health inside the class rather than repeating logic across systems. Enums complement these types by providing named constants for discrete categories, which we’ll use shortly for states. A common beginner error is to keep many globals or pass dozens of primitives between functions; grouping fields reduces parameter lists and avoids inconsistent updates. As an example, a Player class with methods like TakeDamage or ChangeWeapon centralizes side effects and helps maintain a valid state. When designing types, prefer composition: make a Position struct inside Player rather than having global X and Y values. This approach makes saving, copying and testing simpler because you can serialize or clone a single object.

Enums are a simple but powerful C++ feature for naming a fixed set of options. When modeling states, an enum gives you readable labels such as Idle, Walking, Jumping, Attacking, and Dead. Compared to magic numbers or strings, enums are type-safe, easier to refactor, and far less error‑prone. For example, testing if currentState == PlayerState::Jumping is clearer and safer than checking an integer code or comparing strings at runtime. A common misconception is that enums are only for small values; in games they act as the canonical list of allowed states, making it explicit what an entity can do. Enums also make debugging easier because the names show up clearly when converted to strings for logging. One limitation to note: if you need many combinations of simultaneous properties, enums alone are not the right tool—use them to represent mutually exclusive states. For orthogonal properties like 'isInvincible' or 'hasDoubleJump', keep separate booleans or flags, but be careful to avoid contradictory combinations. The key is to use enums for the primary mode of an entity and separate fields for independent modifiers. Using enums to name discrete states means use enums to represent mutually exclusive states clearly and safely; avoid using them for independent modifiers.. In practical terms, why enums beat magic numbers and strings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A finite state machine is a clear, mathematical pattern for modeling behavior where an entity can be in exactly one of a finite set of states at any time. The FSM pattern has three parts: a list of states (usually an enum), rules to change from one state to another (transition guards), and state-specific behavior executed each update. In games, this maps directly to behaviors like Idle, Walking, Jumping and Attacking. The ChangeState method enforces transition rules — for example, preventing switching out of Dead — and can run entry and exit actions like starting or stopping animations. The Update method inspects currentState and executes only the logic for that state. This organization prevents contradictory behavior such as being both Idle and Attacking when not permitted. A common misconception is that FSMs remove all complexity; they don't. FSMs reduce complexity by centralizing state logic, but you still need to design transitions and consider orthogonal modifiers such as temporary invincibility. As a simple exercise, imagine an enemy that can patrol, chase, and attack: the transitions occur when player proximity crosses thresholds. FSMs make those rules explicit and easier to maintain.

This code example ties the concepts together. The enum lists valid PlayerState values. The Player class stores currentState and health and implements ChangeState with guards so the Dead state cannot be reversed. Update contains a switch on currentState to run behavior specific to each mode. TakeDamage decreases health and uses ChangeState to transition to Dead when appropriate. Studying this pattern helps you see how entry and exit logic can be added later, for example to start animations when entering a state. As you read the code, notice how ChangeState prints transitions for debugging and how Update contains placeholder comments where movement and animation code would run. A common learner mistake is to scatter state checks across systems — here we keep state logic centralized in the Player class so state transitions and their effects are easy to trace. Try mentally adding a new state such as Dashing: add the enum, a case in Update, and guard any transitions in ChangeState. That modularity is the real power of the FSM approach. Player FSM: Full example code means a player fsm organizes state, transition guards, and state-specific updates in one place for easier debugging and extension.. In practical terms, a real c++ player class with enum, changestate, update, and takedamage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ChangeState is the gatekeeper for your FSM. It decides when transitions are allowed, runs optional exit logic for the old state and entry logic for the new state, and updates the current state variable. A minimal ChangeState checks for no-op transitions first and returns if the state is already the same. Next, include guards to prevent invalid transitions — for example, avoid moving out of Dead unless your design supports resurrection explicitly. Implementing entry and exit hooks lets you stop the previous animation, reset movement variables, and start the new animation and sound effects consistently. A common mistake is to mix entrance logic into Update or other systems, which scatters responsibilities and leads to subtle timing bugs. For example, if you start an attack animation in Update and also in ChangeState, you may trigger it twice. Structure ChangeState so it does only state transition tasks and leave continuous per-frame behavior to Update. As a practical check, add debug prints to ChangeState during development and verify that each transition happens only once when expected. How would you implement an onEnter and onExit system for each state in your codebase?

The Update method executes the logic appropriate to the entity’s current state on every frame. Implement Update with a switch on currentState so each state’s behavior is grouped together. For instance, in Walking you apply movement velocity and play a walking animation, while in Jumping you apply a vertical impulse and track airborne time. This keeps state code localized and avoids conditionals scattered across the codebase. Include short comments or placeholder calls for physics, animation, and collision checks so you remember to add those systems later. This hands-on activity walks you through adding realistic jump timing to the Player FSM. The goal is to prevent transitioning from Jumping to Idle immediately; instead, the Player should remain in Jumping until a jump duration elapses. Start by adding a float member jumpTimer initialized to zero and a constant JUMP_DURATION, for example 0.8 seconds. Modify ChangeState so entering Jumping resets jumpTimer to zero. Then update the Jumping case in Update to increment jumpTimer by deltaTime each frame and check whether it exceeds JUMP_DURATION; if so, call ChangeState to go to Idle or Walking. This pattern simulates time in the air and enables other checks such as disabling double jumps until the timer allows it. A common pitfall is forgetting to reset jumpTimer when re-entering Jumping, which can cause the player to land immediately. After implementing, simulate frames in main with a fixed delta and print state transitions to verify behavior. This exercise demonstrates how FSMs and timers interact to produce believable movement, and practicing it will make adding other timed actions like attack windup or cooldowns straightforward. Beginners often model behavior with multiple booleans: isWalking, isJumping, isAttacking. At first this seems simple, but these flags can combine into contradictory states — for example, both isWalking and isJumping true unless special code prevents it. FSMs, by contrast, enforce a single canonical mode so such contradictions cannot arise without explicit design. FSMs centralize state logic in one place, improving readability and making it easier to add or change behaviors. That said, booleans still have a place: for independent modifiers like isInvincible or hasDoubleJump, flags are appropriate. The comparison is: FSMs for mutually exclusive primary modes, flags for orthogonal modifiers. A second advantage of FSMs is maintainability: adding a new mode means adding a single enum value, a case in Update, and any necessary transition rules in ChangeState. With booleans you must find every location that sets or reads flags and update them, increasing the chance of bugs. As a concrete test, try converting a system that used booleans into an FSM and notice how many fewer cross-checks you need. Which parts of your current project better fit an FSM and which should remain as flags?

In ChasingPlayer, the enemy moves toward the player and checks if it's within attack range; if so, call ChangeState(Attacking). In Attacking, perform the attack and, if the player moves out of range, transition back to ChasingPlayer, or if the player escapes entirely, transition to Patrolling. Remember three guiding concepts from this chapter. First, game state is the full snapshot of all runtime values, including hidden timers and AI memory — not just what you see on screen. Second, model state using C++ primitives when appropriate, and prefer structs or classes to group related data so you can pass and save objects cleanly. Third, use enums and a finite state machine for mutually exclusive modes, with ChangeState guarding transitions and Update executing state-specific behavior. Together these practices make your game easier to reason about, test, and extend. As you code, ask: could this belong to the single source-of-truth snapshot, and does this behavior belong inside a state case or a separate flag? Keep these three reminders handy as you code: first, list and group the fields that make up a snapshot before you start any save or sync feature. Second, prefer enums for mutually exclusive modes and separate flags for orthogonal modifiers; this avoids contradictions. Third, implement ChangeState and Update consistently — use ChangeState for transitions and entry/exit work, and Update for per-frame behavior and timers like jumpTimer. These habits save debugging time and make adding new behaviors less risky.
